Business.title: European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’
Business.text:
Canada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

In an unprecedented offer, von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the EU and Canada “see the world with the same eyes” through shared democratic values and common approaches to many big issues, from AI to climate breakdown, the Ukraine war and geopolitics.

Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at the European parliament in Strasbourg, she said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”

Carney, who is due to address the parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.

He later tweeted: “Canada and the EU are natural partners, united by shared values. With President von der Leyen and [the European parliament] President [Roberta] Metsola, we focused on what comes next: a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples.”

The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop the future relationship.

Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU.

Von der Leyen said the existing EU-Canada trade deal would be upgraded to an “alliance for the future” to create a “common prosperity and economic security space”.

She said the two sides would also create a tech alliance, integrate defence industrial bases and make the Arctic a “flagship joint project”. EU officials are especially interested in Canada’s energy and natural resources. Von der Leyen pitched joint work on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market.

When the UK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market. The EU also staunchly defended unpicking the four freedoms of its internal market – freedom of goods, services, people and capital.

Carney is expected to get a rapturous reception when he gives his own address to the European parliament. His approach to dealing with Trump has attracted widespread praise among MEPs.

Last month, Carney announced he was breaking off trade talks with the US, saying Canada would not be subjugated, and then introduced retaliatory tariffs on billions worth of US goods. By contrast, the EU last year accepted 15% tariffs on many European goods while dropping its own duties to avoid a trade war with Trump.

Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said “for sure” the EU had lessons to learn from Carney’s approach, because “Trump respects people who are strong”. He added: “Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship.”

Caney’s speech at Davos, where he said there was a rupture in the international order and “middle powers” needed to unite, has also been widely praised. European officials, however, reject the suggestion that the EU, a bloc of 450 million people, is a “middle power”.

Sore points likely to be addressed include 10 EU member states, including France, Poland and Italy, having failed to ratify the EU-Canada trade deal, nearly 10 years after it was struck in 2016.

The offer of associate membership is certain to raise questions among other EU allies, including the UK, which has long sought a more flexible approach from Brussels.

Martin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.

He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.

Business.title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
Business.text:
AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.

Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.

The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to “slow down”.

However, Donald Trump dismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.

In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”

The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.

Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday.

“It’s a hoax,” Trump said via speaker phone to the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.”

The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Presse reported on Monday.

Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.

Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.

In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.

There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.

Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

His claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.

The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.

Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.

And Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder, told the BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.

Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.

Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.

Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.

Despite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.

“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.

“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.

“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”

Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.

The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year.

Business.title: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off
Business.text:
US government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market.

The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel.

With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023.

It comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by a series of drone attacks that have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day.

The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway.

The rise was also fuelled by the Gulf states postponing a meeting with Tehran to discuss creating a temporary shipping lane through the strait of Hormuz, a vital channel through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.

Traders in the kingdom have warned it will run out of oil stocks for export if it does not reopen the east-west pipeline within days.

Gas prices also climbed higher on Monday, with the UK benchmark rising by 5% to 208.73p a therm – its highest level since December 2022.

It came despite Donald Trump on Monday announcing a deal between Ukraine and Russia not to hit each other’s energy targets, while insisting that he believed a politically sensitive rise in US diesel fuel prices was being driven by the conflict in Europe rather than the war in Iran.

With fears mounting as the Middle East war escalates, bond markets have come under intense selling pressure. The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets, meaning a jump in borrowing costs for Washington has consequences for countries, businesses and households worldwide.

Borrowing costs also rose across Europe on Monday, including a rise in 30-year UK government yields to the highest level since March 1998.

The moves come as traders await decisions on interest rates from the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of England on Thursday after the European Central Bank raised borrowing costs last week.

With investors anticipating an increase from the Fed and a hold decision from Threadneedle Street amid mounting inflationary pressures, analysts said global bond markets could face another week of renewed volatility.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “Markets are starting the week on a defensive footing, with the combination of another escalation in the Middle East and increasingly hawkish central-bank expectations weighing on risk appetite.”

With wholesale energy prices on the rise, the cost of petrol and diesel hit new Iran war highs on Monday, according to the RAC, with the average cost of petrol climbing to 169.68p and diesel hitting 191.68p.

The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East this year, sending the oil price soaring from its prewar level of about $72 a barrel to peak at $126 in April.

Brent crude later fell back over the summer amid hopes of a lasting ceasefire, before starting to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart.

After a recent stepping-up of hostilities the benchmark again rose above the $100 a barrel threshold last week for the first time since July.

Chris Beauchamp, of the broker IG, said a “move back to the spring highs” looked increasingly likely. “Oil markets are being subjected to their worst fears all at once – attacks on energy infrastructure, the closure of Hormuz and a breakdown in attempts to restart negotiations,” he said.

“The risk of further disruption is also spreading beyond the Gulf, with the threat of renewed Houthi attacks on shipping adding another layer of uncertainty around key energy and trade routes.

“The major surprise is how calm markets remain in the face of all this, but if prices breach the March highs, things could get ugly very quickly.”

Sports.title: VAR controversy: Pressure for quick decisions obvious in rushed derby review
Sports.text:
"Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"

The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby.

No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen.

Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball.

The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0.

Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR.

The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season.

Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy?

The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent.

"Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!"

It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate.

Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable.

In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions.

This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error.

City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe.

"To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca.

"Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job."

Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act.

There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go.

VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season.

Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly.

Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus.

Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase.

Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology.

This should not have happened.

The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact.

They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at.

By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside.

Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential.

The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete".

Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short.

There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso.

Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes.

Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure.

Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso.

There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol.

Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.

It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off.

Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.

But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure.

There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition.

Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials.

All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.

One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.

Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer.

Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is.

The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.

Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.

Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.

One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.

At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.

Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.

That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.

The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes.

But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.
Sports.description: "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!" The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby. No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors...

Sports.title: Man Utd: JJ Gabriel wants to leave - what happens now?
Sports.text:
Before what was intended to be a historic night at Old Trafford, Manchester United are still digesting the reality that JJ Gabriel wants to leave.

The club have been left reeling at the sudden downturn in relations.

Only a week ago Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut at Leigh that seemed to be the prelude to becoming United's youngest player in history by making his debut against Brighton in the Carabao Cup third round on Wednesday.

Now United are scrambling. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are involved in talks they hope will result in their 15-year-old reversing his plan and choosing to stay.

It feels like a forlorn task.

A belief that promises have been broken and a certainty over Gabriel's current abilities and eventual destiny mean trust is low.

Real Madrid, Barcelona and Paris St-Germain are among the European heavyweight clubs monitoring the situation.

So what happens next?

Gabriel's potential is well known.

All England's leading clubs have seen it first hand given he was named Under-18 Premier League player of the year last season, even though he was only 14 when the campaign began.

He scored 23 goals in the Premier League Under-18 competition and three in the FA Youth Cup. He was the star man in a United side that reached the Premier League Under-18 cup final and the FA Youth Cup final. He was the Premier League Under-18 Player of the Year and United's Under-18 Player of the Year.

The achievements and accolades were in recognition of a player who has balance, pace, close control and a powerful shot. This season he has shown a willingness to get stuck in to try and win the ball back.

"The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how the forward was described by one United source recently.

United Under-21s coach Adam Lawrence made a salient point in the aftermath of that Uefa Youth League victory over Sabah FK.

"The first thing in my job is not to ruin him," said Lawrence. "When you have a talented player like JJ, you obviously don't want to stifle their freedom and their creativity."

Talent like that grabs attention and is not confined to these shores. Real, Barcelona and PSG focus on elite youth players. That is what is happening here.

This is where is gets tricky.

United's initial response to the publicity around Gabriel's future was to say privately that they would try to persuade him his future was best served staying where he is.

They also advised that Gabriel's registration with them runs until the end of the season.

That may well buy them time when it comes to potential moves to Premier League rivals. But what about European giants?

Gabriel has a European Union passport. His mother is of Greek-Cypriot heritage and his father won two caps for the Republic of Ireland.

In 2016 the Court of Arbitration for Sport rejected an appeal by Argentine club Velez Sarsfield - who tried to block one of their 16-year-old players moving to Manchester City - on the basis he was a dual Argentine-Italian national and, as an EU national, should be allowed to transfer to a club within the European Union even though he was coming in from an external country.

West Brom received no compensation when a 16-year-old Louie Barry left for Barcelona in 2019 as Fifa ruled that West Brom failed to formally offer him a scholarship.

West Brom had claimed 130,000 euros (£111,000) in training compensation. Barry left Barca for Aston Villa for just under £1m six months later.

The worst-case scenario for United is Gabriel walks away when he turns 16 on 6 October and they end up with no compensation for a player whose market value, even at this tender age and with so much promise unfulfilled, can be measured in millions.

In the past 24 hours there has been a backlash against Gabriel and his family, for the direction he is taking and around his professionalism and attitude.

Sources close to the player believe this is massively unfair and overlooks the dedication and commitment which means he is so well-regarded by so many clubs.

In addition, he is not the first young player to have a difference of opinion over their future direction with their club.

Jadon Sancho was 17 when he stopped training at City to force through a £10m move to Borussia Dortmund in the belief that he would play more often in Germany than under Pep Guardiola.

Morgan Rogers was Barry's team-mate in the West Brom side that reached the FA Youth Cup semi-final in 2019. Within three months he had left for City, a move completed on his 17th birthday.

Sources feel that, in meetings with the United hierarchy that led to Gabriel committing his short-term future to the club last summer, promises were made over his career path that have not been kept.

He did start to appear in senior training sessions, initially under Ruben Amorim and then Michael Carrick, but speculation around a senior debut last season, which could only be in the FA Cup, was doused by Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher, who had by now taken the senior team manager's role on an interim basis following Amorim's dismissal. Fletcher felt it was too early for Gabriel.

It had been anticipated that Gabriel would feature during United's pre-season programme.

His absence from the trip to Helsinki for a meeting with Wrexham on 18 July was put down to the date he returned for pre-season training.

He was part of every squad after that, but played only once, for eight minutes against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm.

Did that lack of action sow the seeds of discontent? Gabriel travelled to Trondheim for a meeting with Rosenborg on 24 July. Carrick used 11 substitutes that day. Gabriel was one of two United players who did not come on. Five of those who did have left, either permanently or on loan.

It was noted that 18-year-old Tynan Thompson was given a 45-minute senior debut against Leeds United at Croke Park - another game Gabriel travelled to but was not involved in - three weeks after his arrival from Tottenham.

Nevertheless, it was felt Gabriel was likely to become United's youngest player this autumn - probably in the EFL Cup.

While the third-round draw delivered an Old Trafford rematch with Brighton, United's Champions League schedule opened up another avenue.

It is conceivable that Azerbaijani champions Sabah could be the least difficult home game Carrick's side have this season.

United were 3-0 up at half-time and Carrick had used all five substitutes by the 72th minute.

But Gabriel was not among them. As with Max Dowman at Arsenal last season, Uefa's registration rules meant that, because he was 15, Gabriel could only feature if he was named on United's A list of players.

It is not entirely clear why that did not happen. United named a maximum of 25 players, but among them was midfielder Manuel Ugarte, who will not play until after the registration window opens again in January because of a knee injury. Thompson was also on the list.

United coaches have previously suggested that Gabriel is not yet at the physical level required to be a senior player. Sources close to the player reject this.

They also cite Sir Matt Busby's saying "if you are old enough, you are good enough", and see how Arsenal gave Dowman his chance at 15 and Bayern Munich gave Lennart Karl his debut at 17 - and wonder why United have not done the same.

Sports.title: Matt Fitzpatrick: DP World Tour Championship defending champion not comfortable with Dubai location
Sports.text:
Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.

Fitzpatrick is concerned that the United Arab Emirates could be a target in the ongoing conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel.

"You've only got to look at the hotel that got hit earlier this year," Fitzpatrick told BBC Sport. "I was having dinner the week I won in that hotel.

"That's obviously very scary when you think about how it was a few months away but how close you were to that particular spot and for something like that to happen. It's obviously quite scary."

Fitzpatrick would like to see the event switched to a different host country, a decision he called a "no brainer, in my opinion" before adding: "But I'm not a sponsor, I'm not paying the bills and all that sort of stuff.

"I'm sure there's more to it than just the meets the eye."

Led by chief executive Guy Kinnings, DP World Tour officials are assessing safety issues for their final two play-off events in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai.

Both tournaments are backed by key sponsors of the European-based tour and provide a lucrative end to the season for the circuit's leading money winners.

"I think it's annoying, but at the same time, Guy Kinnings can't control what Iran are doing," Fitzpatrick added.

"It is frustrating because as someone who likes to plan and be prepared, it is difficult to kind of figure out what's going on. Obviously, things as they stand are a bit weird over there.

"I can't say I'm like 100% comfortable, but I guess you just have to see nearer the time and, you know, I still need to qualify as well."

Fitzpatrick's Ryder Cup team-mate Shane Lowry said the tour faces important choices over how to end the current season. "They are huge decisions for everyone," said last week's winner of the Irish Open.

"I'm not going to sit here and comment on the whole thing because I think it's up to the powers above to sort that all out. I think if the tournaments are on, the players are going to go. And if they are not, they will find an alternative."

A spokesperson for the DP World Tour said: "We are in constant dialogue with our members and their management teams about the tournaments they play in, but ultimately players' individual schedule choices are a matter for them to decide.

"As far as our play-offs are concerned, it remains our intention to play as scheduled in the UAE but we continue to monitor the situation and take advice from our international travel advisors."

Sports.title: Vini Jnr, Mbappe and Konate obscure Ceuta message ahead of Real Madrid match
Sports.text:
Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.

Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.

Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.

While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan.

Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities.

This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause.

The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa.

Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

The representatives of the players have been asked for comment.

The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time.

Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game.

The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign.

Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended.

Sports.title: FPL: Ranking the most iconic fantasy football picks ever
Sports.text:
Scanning the newspaper, inky fingers and fuzzled minds, scrambling for the calculator and jotting down the codes for Julian Dicks and Juninho. These lads will carry the team until you remember to pick up the house phone and cash in a transfer a few months down the line.

Before templates and triple captains there was a world of fantasy football that existed by writing out your XI and ringing in the names. Parents used it as a summer-holiday maths lesson.

Yet whether in print or online, there's nothing quite like the satisfaction of unearthing an absolute bargain. That free-kick taking defender, the undervalued forward, out-of-position goal-getter or cheap keeper posting clean sheets.

Since it began for the 2002-03 season, Fantasy Premier League has evolved into a huge database boasting millions of players across the globe, with substitutions and wildcards and the maths done for you.

But who, over the past quarter of a century of the competition's official game, are the biggest icons of all time?

With the help of our resident FPL expert Thomas Woods and some extensive research by the Fantasy Football Scout, that's what I'm digging into this week.

Based on stats and a touch of sentiment - Michu, we see you - I've ranked my top 10 below. We'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments, too.

Firstly, let's look at what makes a player iconic. Is it purely posting massive numbers? Thierry Henry's total from the inaugural season, for example, still ranks seventh overall. Indeed the Arsenal man was top scorer in three of the first four campaigns, but also the most expensive.

Frank Lampard, arriving late in the box, topped the charts three times with his goals from midfield for Chelsea, while the twinkle-toed Cristiano Ronaldo did it twice at Manchester United. The pair rank fourth and fifth for best individual seasons, respectively.

It's tempting to say we should discount such "obvious" picks for this debate, but then there's Mo Salah. The Liverpool asset might have eaten up a decent chunk of your budget, but packed guaranteed points for those premium pounds.

As the Fantasy Football Scout explains, since the game began, 52 players have reached 200 points in a season at least once. Salah has done it eight times. And the Egyptian is the only player to ever top 300 points. In fact, he's done it twice.

So Mo probably deserves a go. But we're really searching for those who have offered the most value over the years - cheap picks who seriously delivered.

Some went on to become Premier League stars, others became cult heroes, one-season wonders or bargain buys who got virtual tongues wagging.

10. Harry Kane, Tottenham, 2014-15, starting price £5m

England captain and record goalscorer, three-time Premier League Golden Boot winner. Harry Kane was hardly a secret at Tottenham, right?

After a series of loans and having not yet established himself at White Hart Lane, the young Spurs striker began the 2014-15 campaign as a likely £5m back-up to Emmanuel Adebayor and Roberto Soldado.

Kane didn't find the net until November in the Premier League, a 90th-minute winner after coming off the bench at Aston Villa, but it was the first of 21 goals in the competition that season as the homegrown striker established himself in Mauricio Pochettino's side.

As the Fantasy Football Scout notes, an eight-match run from gameweek 18 to 25 saw Kane notch 77 points with nine goals, four assists and 16 bonus points.

For those who gambled on him early, Kane proved a bargain. He rose from £5m to a peak £6.4m, racking up 191 points and ranking 11th on the all-time value list, despite playing fewer minutes than all those above him.

8. Michel Vorm, Swansea, 2011-12, £4m

Michel Vorm conceded four goals on his Premier League debut. That stacks up for a £4m keeper, you might think. Yet the Dutchman made 11 saves that day at Manchester City, more than anyone else would manage in a single game that season.

Vorm swept Swansea City's end-of-term awards but also became a FPL legend in the process. He made saves but also kept clean sheets, 14 of them in total, and earned the second-most points for a goalkeeper behind City's Joe Hart, who started the game £3m more expensive.

The Dutchman peaked in price at £5.3m and was the fourth-most owned player in the game at one point. Both virtually and in real life, it would be his standout season.

7. Stuart Dallas, Leeds, 2020-21, £4.5m

Under Marcelo Bielsa, Stuart Dallas was a FPL dream.

Racking up defensive clean sheets while operating further forward than his listed position suggested, cheap as you like, and even doing it against league heavyweights Manchester City, where he scored twice for 17 points.

"The Northern Ireland international's versatility played into the hands of FPL managers because, even though he was a classified as a defender, he played all over the place for Leeds in 2000-21 - more often than not as an attacking midfielder," explains Woods.

"And for a starting price of £4.5m you got eight goals, 12 clean sheets, three assists and a total of 171 points. Bargain."

6. Michail Antonio, West Ham, 2019-20, £7m

Michail Antonio is a curious pick, but deserves FPL cult hero status for one of the most memorable months in the game's history.

Classified as a midfielder but deployed up front, Antonio's value actually dropped during a campaign that was disrupted by injury and the coronavirus pandemic.

Following the restart, Antonio was unstoppable. He played seven times in July 2020, scoring eight goals. Incredibly, four of those came in West Ham's 4-0 away win at Norwich, where the midfielder posted a 26-point haul.

That's the joint-most on record for a player valued under £7m, alongside Cole Palmer, and only three off Salah's overall record for a single gameweek.

5. John Lundstram, Sheffield United, 2019-20, £4m

Lord Lundstram, as he was fondly known, didn't notch a season total as high as some on this list, but his bargain price, out-of-position listing and the fact he seemingly appeared from nowhere, having only made five starts for the Blades the previous season, saw him achieve legendary status in FPL.

"A £4m defender is usually the last spot on FPL managers' benches but Lundstram was misclassified by FPL towers and was actually a box-to-box midfielder," says Woods.

"He scored five goals and delivered four assists while picking up clean sheets along the way to 144 points, with his two-goal 21-point haul in week 11 particularly memorable.

"And being able to start a £4m asset allowed managers to cram more talent into the rest of the team too."

4. Riyad Mahrez, Leicester, 2015-16, £5.5m

Riyad Mahrez was a goldmine for Claudio Ranieri and FPL bosses alike during Leicester's title-winning season. As the Fantasy Football Scout notes, he flew out of the blocks with a 15-point haul in week one against Sunderland, rewarding the 5.9% of managers who started the season with the winger in their side.

It was no fluke. Mahrez made double figures in five of the opening six gameweeks, his 56 points among the best starts ever to a FPL campaign. Inevitably, other managers jumped on board, and by week seven Mahrez was in more than 50% of teams.

Jamie Vardy, of course, had a dazzling season of his own, returning a goal or an assist for 15 weeks on the bounce, though he started £0.5m more expensive than his team-mate.

Mahrez finished the campaign as the top scorer in FPL with 240 points, despite his modest starting price.

3. Michu, Swansea, 2012-13, £6.5m

Of course, there is a certain amount of nostalgia and sentiment to FPL. We gaze proudly at these little icons clocking up points like they're family.

Michu was the epitome of an on-screen cult hero, going from relative unknown to bagging 190 points, his price rising by £2m throughout the year.

As Woods says, he is probably the biggest one-season wonder in FPL history.

"A few savvy managers picked up on the fact the Spaniard had scored 15 goals in La Liga the season before and had him on the opening day when he scored twice at QPR," adds our resident FPL expert.

"He was effectively a £6.5m striker classified as a midfielder. It felt like he was in most managers' teams by the time he ended 2012-13 with a whopping 18 goals.

"He managed two the following season... and then left for Napoli."

2. Mohamed Salah, Liverpool, 2024-25, £12.5m

OK, firstly, other Liverpool assets were perhaps unfortunate to miss out on this list - flying full-backs Trent Alexander-Arnold and Andy Robertson were consistently must-have picks.

Luis Suarez, meanwhile, boasts the third-highest score ever and, as the Fantasy Football Scout points out, he notched a record 55 attacking returns in 2013-14 despite missing the first five games.

But if we can allow one premium pick, it has to be Salah. And if we have to pick a season, it must be his record-breaking 2024-25 campaign when the Egyptian produced a staggering 344 points.

Remarkably, it came off the back of his lowest score the year before - although low for Mo was still upwards of 200 points. Salah, simply, is FPL royalty.

1. Cole Palmer, Chelsea, 2023-24, £5m

You have to put Cole Palmer's 2023-24 season into context. He wasn't a household name, like now, having left Manchester City for more gametime at Chelsea.

The youngster began the season as a £5m midfielder and did not start a game for the Blues until matchweek seven. In fact, as the Fantasy Football Scout explains, only 63,575 managers owned him (0.6%) for his first double-figure return at Burnley the following week.

That crept up to 4.5% for his next 12-pointer at Tottenham in gameweek 12, which then triggered a surge in popularity as FPL bosses lumped on Stamford Bridge's new star.

More than five million owned Palmer when he scored four goals against Everton during a 26-point haul in gameweek 33, albeit he still only cost £6.1m.

"Based on starting price, Cole Palmer in 2023-24 is the best-ever value player in Fantasy," concludes the Scout.

Palmer finished as the season's top scorer with 244 points and was handed the biggest price rise in FPL history of £5.5m, meaning he cost £10.5m at the start of the 2024-25 campaign.

Sports.title: What's gone wrong for Chelsea talent Kendry Paez?
Sports.text:
Attacking midfielder Kendry Paez has finally pulled on a Chelsea shirt, three years after agreeing a move to Stamford Bridge - albeit for the club's Under-21s.

Chelsea agreed a £17.27m deal to sign Paez from Ecuadorian side Independiente del Valle in 2023 when he was 16, but his development has not progressed as quickly as many expected.

Now 19, Paez made his first appearance in Chelsea colours for Cobham Next Gen, the club's newly-renamed Under-21 side, as a 12th-minute substitute in a 4-1 win away to Arsenal on Saturday.

It comes after new manager Xabi Alonso said the midfielder was "not in my plans" and Chelsea listed him as an academy player on the club website.

Chelsea explored the possibility of a loan move in English football, but Fifa regulations left the club unable to send him overseas after using all six of their available international loan slots.

With 27 caps for Ecuador, an appearance at this summer's World Cup and a reputation as one of South America's brightest young talents alongside Blues team-mate Estevao Willian, what has happened to Paez?

Paez is a record breaker and a headline maker.

He became the youngest debutant and goalscorer in Ecuadorian top-flight history at the age of 15 before making his debut in the Copa Libertadores, South America's equivalent of the Champions League, later that same season.

Later in 2023, aged 16 years and 131 days, he made his second appearance for Ecuador, becoming the second-youngest South American international to feature in World Cup qualifying after Diego Maradona.

A month later, he became the youngest South American to score in a World Cup qualifier in a 2-1 win away to Bolivia.

It was understandable, therefore, that Chelsea believed the attacker, who had two international goals and 18 caps when they agreed to sign him, was destined for big things.

Chelsea allowed him to train regularly with the first team before he was officially eligible to join the club following his 18th birthday.

They also provided security for Paez, his family and the family of international team-mate Moises Caicedo after violence broke out in Ecuador in early 2024.

A few months later, Paez was filmed in a New York strip club while away on international duty.

He initially impressed on loan at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg by winning September's Young Player of the Month award in the French top flight, but then came in for criticism from then-manager Liam Rosenior.

"We expect more, clearly," Rosenior said later that season. "I'm tired of using the excuse of the player's youth."

Despite Strasbourg's links to Chelsea through their shared ownership, the loan was cut short after one goal in 21 appearances. Instead, he joined Argentine giants River Plate on a two-year loan spell.

Sources in Argentina expressed similar concerns about his attitude when asked by BBC Sport. They point to a disappointing display in the 1-0 Superclasico defeat by fierce rivals Boca Juniors at the Monumental in April.

Shortly afterwards, Paez was named by club president Stefano Di Carlo as one of 15 players training away from River Plate's first team, although other sources felt he could have been given more opportunities.

His loan ended by mutual consent after Paez scored once in 14 appearances in 461 minutes for River Plate.

Ahead of the international break, concern has been expressed in Ecuador, having built him up as the country's next great attacking talent.

Michel Deller, the owner of Independiente, told Hincha Amarillo: "He's like a son to us. We care about him deeply.

"He's a good kid who's had a tough time and has made decisions that have complicated his life.

"We are always hopeful he'll show his exceptional talent one again but right now, it's up to him to decide what to do with his life."

These concerns are not dismissed completely by Chelsea or Paez's environment. However, there is a belief they are grossly overstated, highlighting he is owed time to grow as a player and person.

There was one reminder of Paez's quality in the dying moments of Cobham Next Gen's (Chelsea Under-21s) defeat at Wycombe Wanderers in the EFL Trophy on Tuesday.

It was an outswinging cross from a short corner routine, which Harrison Bettoni tapped in during added time. He then put in another cross that caused havoc as Chelsea chased an equaliser in front of just 778 fans.

It was a much-needed boost for Spanish-speaking Paez, who appeared to stand alone from the other academy players before kick-off.

He did join in their warm-ups but mostly kept to himself before coming on in the 62nd minute.

Ultimately Chelsea lost, while Paez was a peripheral figure playing as a right-sided No 10, like Cole Palmer, in a system that mirrored Alonso's back-three shape.

That was until his flurry of activity late on.

Although he's not Chelsea's youngest player, Paez has already made 70 appearances for Ecuadorian side Independiente and more than 100 senior matches in total.

It's something he can fall back on in a more than salvageable situation.

Chelsea have been encouraged by his attitude, having him back in the building at Cobham where he has trained in a stable and elite environment.

There is stability around him as family attended his recent match at Wycombe.

The Blues are also now able to monitor his development more closely, while academy matches are regularly attended by scouts from across the English Football League and beyond.

There is optimism from those close to Paez that he can impress and gain a first loan move in England in January, or one of the six international loan spots will become available for him to go overseas again.

It's more than possible he can rediscover the form that attracted Chelsea in the first place and fulfil the immense potential that made him one of South America's most coveted young talents.

Sports.title: WTA Finals to move to Charlotte in United States from 2027 on three-year deal
Sports.text:
The American city of Charlotte in North Carolina has been chosen as the new home of the season-ending WTA Finals.

The WTA says it wants to create the "Super Bowl of women's sports" and is hoping the three-year deal will bring more stability to an event that has had six hosts in seven years.

A planned 10-year stay in Shenzhen ended after just one year, with Guadalajara, Fort Worth, Cancun and Riyadh all taking turns since. Crowds have often been disappointing.

"The WTA has always owned the WTA Finals, but now we are going to operate it, too," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo.

"We are not going to do everything ourselves, but we are taking control of this event, of the creation of the revenue and the controlling of the expenses. And that allows us to control our own destiny."

This year's Finals will be held in Indian Wells, California, before the tournament moves to Charlotte from 2027.

Prize money is yet to be announced, but the pot for this year's Finals will be $10m (£7.4m) - which is $5.5m (£4.1m) less than the sum put up by Saudi Arabia last year.

"2026 is a year of transition for the WTA," Camillo said.

"We are doing the normal belt tightening you would expect of any business while also absorbing the unexpected cost of relocating the WTA Finals to Indian Wells.

"What is most important to know is that we have a clear path to deliver consistent, sustainable financial performance in 2027 and beyond, supported by strong revenue and audience growth."

Riyadh had been due to stage the Finals for a third time in November, but the arrangement finished one year early.

This was partly because of the instability caused by the conflict between the United States and Iran, but also reflected the waning interest of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF).

The country's sovereign wealth fund has recently stopped bankrolling LIV Golf, while the Saudi Arabia Snooker Masters was another casualty earlier this year.

The Finals, which involve the best eight singles players and doubles teams of the year, will be staged at the Spectrum Centre where the Charlotte Hornets play their home NBA games.

The basketball season will be in full swing next November and, because of the frequency of home games, the Finals will be reduced from eight days to five, which is likely to affect revenue.

Camillo says the WTA has already started exploring alternative formats with the players, but if the round-robin element of the tournament survives, the finalists would need to play every day.

The WTA will also move its global headquarters from St Petersburg in Florida to Charlotte as part of the agreement.

The WTA says it wants to create the "Super Bowl of women's sports" and is hoping the three-year deal will bring more stability to an event that has had six hosts in seven years. Sports.title: Henry Pollock: Northampton fans on contract stand-off
Sports.text:
Henry Pollock is determined not to blink first in his contractual face-off.

Despite a deal with Northampton being close, amid reports of an agreement of about £400,000 a year,, external the back row stressed on Monday that his renewal was not signed.

He is, he says, still open to offers.

Asked if he was looking forward to the end of the saga, stoked by Pollock's advisor Eddie Hearn, Saints director of rugby Phil Dowson joked that "it would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago".

The haggling has certainly played out more publicly than most negotiations.

Has it taken some of the sheen off a player who was key to Saints winning the Prem title last season and whose public profile has brought new supporters and attention, not just to his club but to his sport in general?

Lis Saunders is the chair of the Northampton Saints Supporters Group.

"I have known Henry coming up through the academy and he is absolutely delightful," she told BBC Sport.

"The perception of his arrogance is wrong. He is just a young bouncy man, living his best life.

"Some people are getting a bit fed up with the whole theatre around [the contract stand-off], though.

"I am laissez-faire about it. If he stays it will be brilliant, but you can't keep someone who wants to go.

"The whole theatre around it is what will grind people's gears. You are starting to see that on some of the fan forums – people saying, 'Either sign or don't. Just don't mess around - we don't need this drama.'"

Saunders points out that, while Pollock can pull a crowd, Saints invariably fill Franklin's Gardens anyway. The turnstiles will carry on clicking at the same rate regardless of his presence.

It would be an emotional wrench rather than a financial loss if he moves elsewhere.

"As the players themselves say, he's an idiot, but he's our idiot," said Saunders.

"We've watched him grow up and he's very much ours. It would be really sad if he didn't stay - perhaps understandable, but really sad."

Charles McGillivray is one of the hosts of Beneath the Lift Tower,, external a Northampton Saints podcast run by fans and named after the landmark that looms over Franklin's Gardens.

He says the stand-off has split fans, even if Pollock, who was superb at the end of last season, still has the support of the majority.

"There are probably two ends of the spectrum," he said.

"You've got some fans who are just reading headlines, may not be as engaged as others and don't really understand the mechanics of how rugby clubs in England work, with the salary cap and things like that.

"But most Saints fans are fairly grounded. They understand that Eddie Hearn coming to Henry Pollock's career is going to be brilliant for the sport and together they're going to make lots of noise.

"And they also understand that the money being quoted [Hearn says Pollock is worth £1m a season] isn't really feasible to be earned by someone in England.

"We think he's a grounded - if ambitious - lad and therefore Northampton is the best place for him to be.

"There isn't a club in England at the moment developing talent at the rate of knots or to the level that Northampton is. And maybe only Bath are having the continued success that Northampton are having."

McGillivray's co-host Simon Stacey, who has been following the club for 40 years, points out that Northampton fans have seen first hand the risks that players run for their rewards.

In 2018 Saints centre Rob Horne went in for a hard but routine tackle and incurred nerve damage that cost him the use of his right arm.

"I don't hold any grudges against Henry," said Stacey. "It doesn't annoy me. I get that they do need to get what they can because it's a short career and they have to look after themselves."

With a club's spending on salaries capped at £6.4m - with another £1.4m available in various credits and compensations - a bumper pay deal for one player at a Prem club reduces the money available for others.

Last autumn scrum-half Alex Mitchell said he and others had prioritised the togetherness, external and quality of Saints' squad over "mega money" elsewhere when opting to re-sign.

While Northampton did not pay up to the salary cap in the most recent report on Prem club finances, which covers the 2024-25 season, a raft of renewals is likely to take them closer to the limit in the coming years.

However, if Pollock's stance is causing ructions in the squad, they are hiding it well.

Fly-half Fin Smith momentarily joined Hearn in lobbying for Pollock to be granted a £1m annual salary this month, telling reporters that "he's worth it" before joking that Pollock had sent him out to do a bit of PR on his behalf.

Dowson dropped a request into the squad's group chat, asking if the squad could borrow the private jet Hearn had laid on for Pollock to visit him on the French Rivera.

As Pollock gave an interview on Monday, soberly stressing that the forthcoming season could be his last at the club, his straight face briefly broke as Mitchell smirked at him from across the room.

Newcastle Red Bulls

The obvious destination were Pollock to move within the Prem.

Backed by Austrian energy drink dynasty, Pollock would be a statement signing that fits their youth-orientated brand. The club had plenty of headroom on the pay roll, spending barely half of the salary cap's upper limit in 2024-25 campaign.

However, a revamp of the playing squad since then will have given them less ability to manoeuvre, and Prem Rugby rules on domestic moves prevent Pollock from being the club's designated marquee player for his first two seasons elsewhere.

Pollock would also have to weigh up whether swapping the Prem champions for the league's bottom club, who are without Champions Cup rugby for 2026-27 at least, is desirable.

French clubs operate under a significantly higher salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m), and the Top14 is booming, challenging football for prominence in the country.

Thanks to skirmishes with Bordeaux-Begles in the Champions Cup, Pollock has pantomime villain status in the country.

He was jeered the loudest of any player when England played France in Paris in March. His vigorous celebrations of Tommy Freeman's 76th-minute try, which appeared to have clinched the win for the visitors, will have further endeared him to the locals.

However, a move across the Channel would come at the cost of Pollock's England career and the associated central contract, worth about £150,000.

There is also a considerable cultural shock to overcome. Courtney Lawes, a Northampton legend, has just returned to England, saying some aspects of his two-season spell with Brive were challenging.

Henry Arundell, the bright, young thing of English rugby before Pollock, endured a difficult time at Racing 92 before returning to the Prem a year earlier than anticipated.

The money-making move of choice for many of the southern hemisphere's finest.

Richie Mo'unga, Pieter Steph du Toit and Malcolm Marx are among those who have enjoyed the lighter schedule and yen-heavy pay days in Japan.

While England internationals George Kruis and Alex Goode have made moves there in the past, there has been a shift lately to favour Japanese players over big-money imports.

Both Kruis and Goode were near the end of their careers. A switch to such relative obscurity would do little to build Pollock's brand in rugby's major markets.

Perhaps the most intriguing comment made by Pollock this week was a desire to explore "other sports" during his career.

He has been a ringside regular since signing with Matchroom, most recently attending Katie Taylor's farewell fight at Dublin's Croke Park, and chatting with UFC fighter Ian Machado Garry at a recent charity fundraising event.

His high-energy style would suit a switch to rugby league, and it has been reported, external that a number of Super League clubs, buoyed by possible investment from the NRL, are monitoring Pollock's situation.

The big-money start-up circuit, originally slated to begin next month, would surely have been keen on Pollock.

However, it has been postponed until 2028 and, with conflict in the Middle East further unsettling investors and logistics, looks increasingly unlikely to transpire.

Sports.title: 2030 Winter Olympics: Venues confirmed including events in French Alps and Netherlands
Sports.text:
The sporting venues for the 2030 Winter Games have been confirmed, with events to be held in Lyon and the French Alps - except speed skating, which will take place in the Netherlands.

Events will take place at 11 competition venues, external primarily across southern France with the location allocation for ice sports and alpine skiing confirmed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC)on Wednesday.

Lyon will host curling, figure skating and short track speed skating across three sites, including Parc Olympique Lyonnais, the home of the Ligue 1 side.

Courchevel will host the Alpine skiing speed events – the downhill and super-G, including team events – while Val d'Isere stages the slalom events.

The announcement finalises the venues after a turbulent few months for 2030 Games organisers, which included several changes to original plans.

In May, they were forced to move the Games' 'ice sports hub' to Lyon from Nice after the south coast city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow Nice's football stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.

And last month, Edgar Grospiron left his position as president of the organising committee just 18 months after his appointment following a turbulent reign amid budget cuts for the Games.

It was also confirmed in May that the long track speed skating events will take place at the Thialf arena in Heerenveen, The Netherlands.

Holding the speed skating in a pre-existing arena outside France was a condition agreed with the IOC when French Alps were awarded the Games in order to reduce costs, as organisers do not want to build new venues that would not have a definite legacy in the host region.

There will be 16 different sporting disciplines, external at French Alps 2030, with freeride skiing and snowboarding, plus synchro9 - synchronised figure skating - added to the Winter Olympics for the first time.

Sports.title: Everton: How James Garner became main man at Goodison Park
Sports.text:
Crunching tackles that help win hard-fought away points in an all-action performance are the kind of things Everton fans have become well accustomed to when watching James Garner.

Now the rest of the Premier League are starting to take proper notice.

Following Everton's goalless draw at Tottenham on Saturday, during which midfielder Garner bested a home line-up boasting the near-£200m midfield pairing of Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, Match of the Day pundit Thomas Frank hailed Garner's display.

It featured crucial challenges on Tonali and Fernandes to halt promising home attacks - by a player who missed a significant part of pre-season after hernia surgery.

"Garner today was extremely good," said Frank. "He is aware; he's talking; he's organising.

"In a high-press situation, he does the recovery, and that's just so exceptional and so important when you are playing against a team who are dominating you.

"He was running so hard, so that's one side of his game, but also so important is his touches. He is a lot on the ball. It's through him that a lot of things are happening."

Fellow pundit and former Everton defender Ashley Williams said: "He's really impressive. If you're a centre-back behind him, he's the type of midfielder you want."

Garner was signed for an initial fee of only £9m from Manchester United in 2022, having spent the previous season on loan helping Nottingham Forest get promoted to the Premier League.

The academy graduate did not make a Premier League start for United.

After taking two seasons to settle at Everton under Frank Lampard and then Sean Dyche amid a backdrop of financial problems and points deductions, the 2025-26 campaign proved to be a watershed moment.

Garner played all but six minutes of Everton's Premier League campaign to spearhead a European push that lasted for much of the season.

In December Everton travelled to Forest with a depleted squad and won 2-0 to move within four points of the top four.

Garner scored Everton's opening goal in a commanding display that underlined his development.

Following that win, manager David Moyes said: "When I came in, I still saw a bit of a boy and I think I now see someone who's turning into a really good leader as well, beginning to take a bit more responsibility and grow up and begin to start to act like a real midfield player."

The data backs up Garner's growing maturity.

He ranked top for a host of metrics for Everton last season, in terms of creativity and physicality, making the most successful passes, tackles and interceptions, but also providing the most assists and engineering the most chances.

Perhaps most impressively, he stepped up in the absence of key winger Jack Grealish - four of Garner's seven assists came after Grealish's season was ended by injury in January.

"He's been fantastic since I came in," said Moyes. "I didn't realise probably how good he was. He's been so good."

Sports.title: Sydney Sweeney: Amy Hunt says advert is barrier to girls in sport
Sports.text:
British sprinter Amy Hunt says she is concerned about the controversial advert starring Sydney Sweeney being part of a "barrier" to girls' participation in sport.

The advert for a sports betting company features the American actress naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.

After running a season's best 22.10 seconds in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday, Hunt said: "This is what women in sport look like."

Hunt, 24, is among several female athletes who have spoken out against the advert's messaging.

"When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like," Hunt told Good Morning Britain.

"When we see the stats of 64% of young girls dropping out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don't need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like - professional or kind of just going to do a Parkrun with your friends.

"So it's about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there, and you don't have to worry what you look like. You don't have to worry about what you're wearing."

Hunt has enjoyed a breakthrough season, winning four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month.

She said "sport is not pretty", describing how she is often sick during sessions or in tears if something does not go to plan.

Hunt said the responses to Sweeney's advert had eclipsed the controversy.

"The reaction has almost outweighed the moment because the first thing I saw was all of the positive compilations of women in sport," she said.

Organisations did not want to comment publicly to BBC Sport on the issue for fear of giving Sweeney and Novig the oxygen of yet more publicity.

Harriet Walker, fashion editor at The Times, told Woman's Hour she felt the advert was regressive.

"When women's bodies are this accessible, the rest of us are taken less seriously and I think using that level of nudity and it's not just nudity, it's provocative sexual poses, it's sort of turning the clock back to when you had naked women advertising cigarettes or women in bikinis on game shows.

"It's using women's bodies as a means to grab and maintain male attention and it is the bodies that are doing the talking, not the women. I find that incredibly depressing."

Sports.title: Watching Cavan Sullivan, excitement is tempered by memories of hypetrains past
Sports.text:
The trouble with trying not to hype up Cavan Sullivan is that he keeps on doing cool stuff. Like this past weekend, when he scampers along on a Philadelphia Union breakaway, loses his man by stopping so suddenly it’s as if he’s pulled a ripcord, back-heels the cutback behind his standing leg, watches it slowly kiss off the far post and in, and celebrated the goal by bowing and doffing an imaginary top hat to the crowd.

Like when he doubles the score by setting up an attack and finishing it himself with a left-footed lash through the goalkeeper’s legs form an acute angle. Like when he fashions yet another goal by holding up the play and then suddenly springs a teammate up the right flank.

And that’s just this past weekend.

It’s hard not to get worked up when an American, two weeks and a day before his 17th birthday, almost matches Lionel Messi for goal involvements in Major League Soccer and the Leagues Cup since the World Cup. When he powers an entire team of grown men to a 10-game unbeaten run. When he breaks Freddy Adu’s record as the youngest Major League Soccer debutant by 13 days, at 14 years and 293 days old. When he has netted six goals and five assists in his last eight matches. When he appears to be on the eve of his first United States men’s national team call-up.

When his swagger and flair are vindicated by the advanced metrics, which suggest that he has already compiled the best MLS season ever by a teenager, outdoing Alphonso Davies. That he is, in fact, the league’s second-best American player right now.

What makes Cavan Sullivan so tantalizing is that he isn’t theoretical.

And yet we wince.

We have been down this road before. That way madness lies, let me shun that – so warned King Lear.

As an American soccer community, we have developed a reflexive recoil against the Godding up of yet another prodigy. Still, it’s hard to resist, even though we know better. From the experience of Bobby Convey, and Jamar Beasley, and John O’Brien, and Jozy Altidore, and Juan Agudelo, and Brek Shea, and Julian Green, and Gedion Zelalem. They had skills and bodies and brains we could dream on, which we never managed to resist.

Did you even remember Green and Zelalem? Green is 31 and presently without a club; Zelalem, now 29, plays for New Mexico United. Both were promised to us as potentially first American male superstar when they emerged from the Bayern Munich and Arsenal academies, respectively. But then, all the men on that list, and so many more, were supposed to be that. None of them were.

We’ve been doing this since the 1970s, when it was decided that Kyle Rote Jr, son of the gridiron football hero, would put soccer on the map. He did indeed become famous, but much less for what he did on a soccer field than for thrice winning the popular gameshow Superstars – wherein top players from different sports competed in a series of athletic events. He led the North American Soccer League in scoring as a rookie and then tailed off, taking a “sabbatical” to lead a hunger relief mission to Cambodia in 1980 and never playing soccer again.

They weren’t all failures. Several had solid professional careers. Altidore had a highly productive spell on the United States men’s national team – he is still its third all-time leading scorer, behind Landon Donovan and Clint Dempsey. His club resume, however, amounts to two good seasons in the Netherlands and half a dozen strong campaigns in Major League Soccer, after he had been discarded by five different European clubs.

There’s still no telling, exactly, what the now-23-year-old Gio Reyna might or might not become. His body hasn’t cooperated, breaking down again and again, and neither has he managed to muster the consistency to become a regular and productive starter on a European club (that may change this season with Strasbourg). He’s bounced around, largely anonymously, briefly resurfacing for World Cups. It feels like a long time ago now, when he was 17 and fit seamlessly into Borussia Dortmund’s attacking diamond with Erling Haaland, Jude Bellingham and Jadon Sancho.

Of all the chosen ones, only Christian Pulisic has really panned out something like we had hoped. He has, however, never really been the focal point in the attack of any of his three European clubs. And he’s developed an odd penchant for falling out of favor after two or three seasons, tumbling down the depth chart at Dortmund and then Chelsea and now Milan. Under new manager Ruben Amorim, Pulisic, the author of 52 goals and assists over the last three Serie A campaigns – albeit notably fewer of them in the 2025-26 season – has been benched and has appeared just once in the Italian league.

And all of them toiled under the looming specter of Adu. More than two decades on from Freddymania, his name is still invoked as a cautionary tale. He works as a personal skills coach now, and has done since last playing professionally five years ago.

So we proceed carefully, taking great pains not to make the same mistakes again.

The thing is, Sullivan has already scored more goals in two-thirds of an MLS campaign than Adu did in his highest-scoring season, his rookie year with DC United in 2004. And the league is a hell of a lot harder to score in these days. It’s better set up to handle transcendent talent, too.

Unlike most of the others, there are real numbers there. Real performances. Real highlight clips, captured at the senior level against credible opposition. Manchester City certainly think he’s real, long ago arranging for his transfer when he turns 18. It’s all there, other than the size of Sullivan himself. That may prove problematic. But then he wouldn’t be the first undersized superstar.

And yet.

Gaming_Tech.title: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity
Gaming_Tech.text:
Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".

Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency".

"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.

The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment.

"AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.

"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."

In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company.

He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.

But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious".

As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed.

This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.

Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".
