Entertainment.title: Ed Sheeran's support acts quit tour in support of Macklemore
Entertainment.text:
All of the remaining support acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour have quit, after the rapper Macklemore was dropped from the line-up for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.

Among them were Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, who said in a statement: "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed."

Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham also announced their departure. Irish folk band Beoga, who perform with Sheeran on stage every night, dropped out too.

The announcements came hours after Sheeran said he would not be drawn into a public debate over Gaza, and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran said on Instagram.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran is set to next perform at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Saturday. His Loop tour website has not been updated, and Graham and Rowe are still listed as special guests.

Earlier this month, Macklemore - real name Benjamin Haggerty - called for a "free Palestine" and showed images of devastation in Gaza during two concerts in New Jersey.

His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to drop him from the tour.

In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken to the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately pulled the plug.

While the star said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and that the "suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy", he also attempted to explain his decision to keep political issues at arm’s length.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.

"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."

He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

Sheeran added that, “as with all my support acts", Macklemore had been allowed to choose his own setlist.

If the statement was meant to placate his fans and other artists on the line-up, it has seemingly had the opposite effect.

Writing on Instagram, Lukas Graham said: "We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them."

Rowe, who opened on the Australian leg of the tour earlier this year and resumed as a support act for the US in June, said he did not "take the decision [to quit] lightly", adding: "Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this."

In their post, Beoga said: "As musicians, playing to those crowds every night is the stuff of dreams but to play in venues that silence anyone advocating for a Free Palestine is simply not an option for us."

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.

The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.

In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts.

Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.

However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.

Tour promoter Messina Touring Group told Rolling Stone that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans".

Many of the acts who withdrew on Tuesday night said Kraft's involvement had influenced their decision.

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation," said Lukas Graham.

"Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge."

In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said artists have a right to speak out about politics, but added that "I do feel for Ed Sheeran".

"I think he's been left in a really difficult decision, stuck between his supporting artists, whom he wants to promote and support, and the promoters, and I hope that people will still go and see his show," she said.

She added that "nobody should be platforming antisemitism", but that people and the promoters were "entitled to take their own views" about whether politics and music should mix.

Elan Carr, chief executive of the Israeli-American Council, told Today that Macklemore's remarks were "outrageous" and had "no place in a concert".

"A concert is supposed to be inclusive, and this is by the way something Mr Sheeran said, he wants inclusive concerts for all his concertgoers. And to make Jewish concertgoers and pro-Israel concertgoers feel unwelcome is a terrible thing to do and that's what Macklemore did, and so it is entirely appropriate that he was excused from further performances."

The situation has sparked much debate, with one caller, Isaac from London, telling BBC Radio 5 Live's Nicky Campbell phone-in that Sheeran "should have cancelled the tour" and "maybe gave some funds to a Palestine relief fund" as well as still paying the tour crew.

But another caller, Deborah, in Sheeran's home county of Suffolk, responded: "But then who suffers? The fans.

"The fans who have organised their life around have going to these concerts. The people who have been looking forward to it for weeks, months, years."

Entertainment.title: Bonnie Greer: British-American author and critic dies at 77
Entertainment.text:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart."

Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting".

He added that she was "a true life force" and he would "never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin" during an appearance with the then-British National Party (BNP) leader on the BBC's Question Time in 2009.

Lammy added: "I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship."

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Greer's voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation".

He said: "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously."

Journalist and broadcaster Sangita Myska, who interviewed Greer several times, recalled her as being a "smart, sassy, firebrand who will be missed from our public discourse".

Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.

Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a powerful panellist on programmes like Newsnight Review and Question Time.

She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).

Once named by the Observer, external as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions.

Entertainment.title: Olu Jacobs: Legendary Nollywood actor dies in Nigeria aged 84
Entertainment.text:
Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.

His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.

Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".

Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.

He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.

"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.

He became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.

His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.

In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.

In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

In 2021, Silva disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy bodies.

"It's a degenerative disease that affects the brain and it's almost like a Parkinson-type of disease - it affects the brain and affects the person," she said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Chude Jideonwo.

On several occasions, there were rumours that Jacobs had died, but his family would promptly debunk them, the latest being in June 2024 when his eldest son, Soji, went on TV to say his father was still alive.

Entertainment.title: Emmys remember Catherine O'Hara, Rob Reiner and Hayden Panettiere
Entertainment.text:
Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star and on-screen mother, Catherine O'Hara, at the Emmy Awards

Culkin remembered her as "our momma", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to", he said.

US singer-songwriter Noah Kahan performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment on the night, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid another emotional tribute to the late actor and director Rob Reiner.

Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek.

Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and David - in Schitt's Creek.

"You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin.

"There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is momma... She was my mom. She was our momma."

He then reminded the audience at Los Angeles' Peacock Theater to "call your mother tonight" and urged them to "give it up for the moms", drawing cheers.

Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, Culkin joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."

Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from their show back at her.

"These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said.

O'Hara's final acting role, as movie executive Patty Leigh in Seth Rogen's satire The Studio, earned her an Emmy and a Golden Globe nomination.

Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."

The emotional moment, which featured a giant image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears.

Rob Reiner, who was killed along with his wife last year, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.

A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer - who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men - on Monday.

She called him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead", a reference to his character in the 1970s US sitcom All in the Family

The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his dad, Carl Reiner.

Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's.

Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Bright Creatures actress Sally Field led a tribute to country music star Dolly Parton, who died last month.

Field, who starred opposite Parton in the 1989 comedy drama Steel Magnolias, described her as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny", as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.

"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021.

"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever."

Entertainment.title: Emmy Awards: Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes history with double win
Entertainment.text:
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.

Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.

On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".

"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding "Diolch yn fawr iawn" - which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.

Other winners of the coveted US TV awards included Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Stephen Colbert, while there was an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a special humanitarian award for Michael J Fox.

Rhys was named best lead actor in a limited series for The Beast In Me, then won best lead actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay.

A small number of actors, including Alan Alda, Sally Field, John Goodman, Elisabeth Moss and Ted Danson, have previously been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year, but Rhys is the first to score a double win.

Backstage, he said: "I'm from a small country, and I'm glad we get moments to kind of put our flag on the map and say, 'we punch higher than our weight sometimes'."

The Beast In Me follows a grieving author, played by Claire Danes, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious new neighbour suspected of murder.

Rhys said it was a "real shock" to win the award, and told Danes: "Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast, you are an intimidating scene partner, but I'm grateful for all this."

Later in the night, accepting the comedy actor prize for playing the mayor in Widow's Bay, he thanked the family, friends and colleagues who supported his career, including his parents who "kicked me on to the stage at a very early age".

His Widow's Bay co-star Kate O'Flynn was among the other British winners, being named best supporting comedy actress for playing Patricia in the show about a fictional island beset by a centuries-old curse.

"I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow's Bay, in front and behind the camera," said O'Flynn, from Bury in Greater Manchester.

She added: "This is the role of a lifetime... Thank you for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia."

Elsewhere, Jean Smart won best comedy actress for her role in the fifth and final series of Hacks.

It is the fifth Emmy she has won for the Hollywood satire. "What a ride this has been," Smart reflected, and joked that the audience only gave her a standing ovation "because I'm old".

It was Smart's eighth Emmy win in total, and The Diplomat's Allison Janney also picked up the eighth Emmy of her career, scoring best supporting actress in a drama series.

Smart and Janney have both now equalled the record for the most acting wins ever, shared with Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus.

Despite her past success, Janney was a surprise winner on Monday and said she was "genuinely shocked" to see off competition from four stars of hospital drama The Pitt, among others.

Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn won the first Emmy of her career for best lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus, the Apple TV show about a woman who discovers almost everyone else in the world has been taken over by a mysterious mind virus.

The Pitt won best drama, traditionally seen as the most prestigious award of the night.

And the show's leading star Noah Wyle also picked up the trophy for best lead actor in a drama series for the second year in a row.

"I'm a Hollywood kid. I was raised on a television, and movie theatres were my place of worship," Wyle told the audience. "This is all I've ever wanted to do and this is the only club I've ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me."

The former ER star praised all of his fellow nominees, but singled out veteran British star Sir Gary Oldman, who was nominated for Slow Horses.

Wyle said he was inspired by Sir Gary's performance as Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious in 1986 film Sid and Nancy, recalling how at the time he thought it was "the benchmark that I want to hit one day in my career".

Michael J Fox was given a standing ovation as he received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his campaigning for support for Parkinson's disease.

The Back to the Future star, 65, who founded the Michael J Fox Foundation in 2000, said: "When it starts getting tough, you show up, you help, and if you get a little joy while you're doing it, that's even better."

Appearing in a wheelchair, he told the audience he initially kept his condition secret after being diagnosed at the age of 29.

"I worried that it would affect my work and my relationships with audiences when they laughed if they knew I was sick," he said.

But he added: "Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease. So I set out to advocate for patients' needs and raise money, and to propel us towards a cure."

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to".

Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."

Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner.

Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.

In other award categories, Scottish TV presenter Alan Cumming accepted the best reality show prize for the US version of The Traitors, an honour he said would encourage the team to "do better and go bigger".

"It is so beautiful that a show about treachery and betrayal brings people together," he joked, as he also thanked his dog Lala, "the perfect co-host".

On an evening otherwise light on political messages, Cumming concluded his speech by encouraging US citizens to register to vote ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Stephen Colbert won best variety series after presenting his final episode of The Late Show in May.

The presenter said nightly talk shows were a "fantastic incubator for young people to come in, work professionally, on a deadline, in collaboration, and that is the future of our business that we have to look after".

He added: "I want to say to the audience, thank you so much for watching, we hope you enjoyed the show, we had a great time doing it for you. That's it, thank you, and catch you on the flip."

Entertainment.title: Trump says Kennedy Center to close as court rules his name must stay off building
Entertainment.text:
The Kennedy Center board has voted to close the performing arts centre for two years, just as a US judge blocked it from adding President Donald Trump's name back to the building.

In May, the same judge ordered the removal of Trump's name and blocked its temporary closure for proposed renovations.

The board, which is chaired by Trump and includes his cabinet members and allies, approved a resolution in August to add the inscription, "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" to the venue.

Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year.

The judge's written order came less than an hour before the centre's board voted on the closure.

This was the third time it has approved closing the centre since February, amid legal challenges to Trump's work to take greater control of the institution, but there is a chance the centre's doors could stay open despite Tuesday's vote.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the venue "for safety reasons".

While the closing "will take place immediately", Trump said renovations cannot begin until the court "rules on the Board's approved name" and vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if it is a "negative" ruling.

He added that the US Department of Justice would ask for an expedited appeal and that he had raised $17m for the centre to "keep it afloat".

Also in August, the board approved a resolution to rename the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100m was raised for the renovations.

Congress has approved more than $250m for renovations, as well.

However, the centre cannot close unless the federal judge, Christopher Cooper, lifts a temporary block that he put in place in May requiring it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty goes ahead.

Cooper had said the board could return and request the block to be lifted, provided it came to the decision to close "in a prudent manner". The request is expected to be made by Friday, CNN reported.

Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and Democrat, said on Tuesday that the centre had planned for years to undergo phased renovations while still putting on some performances, instead of fully shutting.

She blamed Trump's attempted renaming for the departures of audiences and artists, telling the BBC he "only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity".

"That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution."

In February 2025, Trump replaced several trustees on the board, which then decided in December to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the centre's front portico the following day.

The changes were followed by cancellations by artists booked at the venue and a drop in ticket sales.

Entertainment.title: Anniversary excitement builds among Yorkshire Pokémon fans
Entertainment.text:
For most people, Wednesday will be just another day - the midweek hump at school or work. But not for Pokémon fans.

The Japanese brand has become one of the most recognisable in the world, with its colourful creatures appearing in video games and on shop shelves across the globe.

But perhaps most synonymous with the Pokémon phenomenon is its trading card game, which has been played, bought and sold between collectors for the last three decades.

Wednesday marks the release of Pokémon's 30th anniversary range - a day one collector described as the brand's biggest day "in the last decade, if not more".

Gus Hall, owner of Evolution Games in Halifax, said he expected fans to queue before shops open to get their hands on the first release of the cards.

A long-term Pokémon collector himself, Hall said he was "massively excited" about the anniversary range.

"If you want my personal opinion, I would say this is the biggest release for a good while for Pokémon. Some of the products and the cards they've leaked... are crazy," he said.

Pokémon's popularity has exploded over the years, with some cards originally worth just a few pounds now selling for eye-watering amounts.

Hall said a box that may have been worth £200 in the late 1990s would now sell for about £35,000.

As a child, Hall would spend about £1.99 of his pocket money on a new Pokémon card. His parents would "go ballistic" at him for what they believed was a waste of money.

He said: "They'd say to me: 'Why are you wasting your money on these types of things?'… Now I get the exact same from parents who come into my store and say to their children: 'Why are you wasting your money on these [cards]?'… But, you know, look who's laughing now!"

But what has made these cards so popular - and so valuable?

"Pokémon is different to other things in society these days - there's nothing electronic in trading cards," Hall said.

"Parents quite like it because it's healthy; it creates friendships and trading and gaming, and incorporates all these wonderful things that aren't detrimental to a child or young person's mind."

Hall said the satisfaction of collecting a set and "chasing certain cards" in that set was a huge part of the enjoyment, and described the moment of pulling the desired card as "euphoric".

Phoebe Watson, an employee at Evolution Games, has been collecting Pokémon cards for the last 20 years.

She said she was "super excited" for the first release of the anniversary range and was hoping to secure some of the cards, which feature some of her favourite Pokémons.

But Watson is realistic - she expects the first release to sell out quickly.

"It is going to be big. We get collectors in every single day, multiple times a day, and I've had hundreds of people ask me: 'When is the set dropping? Do you know how much you're getting?'."

Drew Emerson, one of Europe's top Pokémon players, told BBC Radio Sheffield he had "travelled all over the world" playing the trading card game.

Emerson said it was going to be "very, very difficult" to secure the anniversary cards on first release, but added the collection was "very, very exciting".

Pokémon is reprinting old, rare cards, Emerson said, and he was "most looking forward" to the release of a Crystal Lugia card.

Lee Glen, owner of trading card stores Rocket's Hideout in York and Selby, said Pokémon cards had "exploded" in the last five years, which he largely attributed to the hobby being "multi-generational".

"I got back into collecting five years ago with my son. It was something nostalgic that I used to do, and then got back into it with my son… You have sons, daughters, mums, everyone - and they can do it together," Glen said.

He said Pokémon was "constantly reinventing" products, and was "really good at bringing people back in".

Glen's York store is usually closed on Wednesdays, but it will open specially for the first release, when Glen too expects customers to flock to York to get their hands on the stock.

Among those hoping to secure some anniversary cards is 21-year-old Grace Orton, who said she was willing to queue up to get her hands on them.

"I'll definitely be trying at some point to get some. I know it'll be really difficult if I'm not [at a shop] immediately", Orton said.

Despite only starting her Pokémon card collection three years ago, Orton said she was "looking to spend quite a bit of money, unfortunately" on the anniversary range.

She said: "It's such a big, sought-after set. A lot of the artwork is really nice; I really want some of it for my personal collection."

Another Pokémon fanatic, Ash Mehr, said he started collecting the cards between 20 and 30 years ago.

After a brief hiatus, Mehr began his collection once again after his son took an interest in Pokémon.

He said: "I feel like I'm sort of dragging my son to these events to try and get the cards, but really it's a little bit of a guilty pleasure of mine! But hopefully, we'll get a good haul and get some good pulls [from the anniversary range]".

There is a huge sense of nostalgia surrounding the 30th anniversary of Pokémon cards, Mehr said, adding: "It takes me back to being a kid, really, something I don't get to enjoy now as much in my early 40s."

But with high-value products comes risk - and Glen has warned of Pokémon fans being scammed around the release of the anniversary range.

He encouraged people to buy the cards from national and independent retailers, and avoid "secondary markets", which may be used to re-sell the cards at "two or three times" the price.

He said: "Just research and know what to spend.

"If it looks too cheap, chances are it is… because of the desirability of a product, people will always try and copy [them]. Do your homework."

Entertainment.title: Your mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakes
Entertainment.text:
By now, we’ve grown used to watching Tom Cruise excel at everything he does. Running in films? The best. Risking his life in action scenes so preposterously dangerous that audiences need to have their sphincters manually unclenched with a crowbar? Absolutely, none better. Singlehandedly ensuring that theatrical exhibition didn’t go extinct after Covid? The man deserves all the praise in the world for that.

But nobody is perfect. Live long enough and a few flaws will worm their way to the surface. This is as true for Tom Cruise as it is for anyone else. And while I realise that this might do me out of a cake this Christmas, the following really needs to be said: Tom Cruise isn’t very good at interviews.

As you will be aware, Cruise’s new film Digger comes out soon. The film is a risk. It is his first original, non-sequel, non-action film in which he co-stars since 2007’s Lions for Lambs. It is also, if the trailers are any indication, palpably batshit. This means that Cruise has to reintroduce himself to the world as an actor, rather than the guy who just flings himself off a variety of increasingly berserk surfaces. And this means promotion. Until this week, that promotion has involved either World Cup-themed promos filmed in character or interviews where the subject matter was almost exclusively limited to lens choice.

However, yesterday Cruise subjected himself to a rare longform interview opposite GQ’s Zach Baron. On paper, it couldn’t have been easier. Baron was a perfectly chosen interviewer for the job, understanding exactly when to flatter and when to needle. However, Tom Cruise’s defences are foot-thick and watertight, and the majority of Baron’s questions simply bounced off him.

This resulted in a fairly unsatisfactory 30-minute stalemate in which Tom Cruise talked and talked and said nothing at all. No matter how hard Baron probed, he was met with a fat wedge of waffle. The clickbait industrial complex has done its best to pick the bones of the interview for a news peg, but the best it seems to have come up with is a variation of “Tom Cruise admits that he can be intense on set”. Which, well, duh.

Aside from that, we simply got a rehash of all the old talking points from every junket he’s done for a decade. He’d rather talk about cinematography than himself. He is constantly trying to learn new skills. He writes down his dreams and how to accomplish them. None of this is new information. It’s all highly frustrating. But it does make sense. As brilliant as he is on screen, behind the scenes Cruise is a carefully managed enigma. This may well be because, the last time he allowed his own self to parade before the press, it ended with couch-jumping and excruciatingly testy interviews about Scientology. It seems unthinkable now, but that press run went so badly that Sumner Redstone ended up effectively firing Cruise from Paramount over it.

It took Cruise years to build himself back up from that, and the results have been spectacular. The Mission: Impossible films have been some of the greatest of his career. Top Gun: Maverick saved Hollywood. He is now in a position of enormous power and authority. So going back out in front of an interviewer is bound to be a risk for him. But one thing is certain. The Digger promotional cycle cannot just be variations of the GQ interview, because too many opaque soundbites will simply end up boring potential audiences rigid. There will be more interviews – he’s thought to be hitting the podcast circuit soon – so he needs to adapt his strategy.

The good news is that one thing Cruise did say in his GQ interview is that, when he sets a goal, he writes down all the steps necessary to accomplish it. This is exactly what he should do here. If his dream is doing press that will make people want to watch Digger, then he knows he will need to work up some new anecdotes – long enough to filibuster, but twisty enough to entertain – while developing a persona that appears to welcome scrutiny while wriggling out from underneath it.

It can be done. Robert Downey Jr is an actor with many areas of his past he would rather not touch in print, and he has built up an incredibly charming suit of armour that allows him to breezily bat questions away when they get too personal. This is exactly what Tom Cruise should be learning to do. Or perhaps not; after all, he has made hundreds of millions of dollars by revealing scarcely anything about himself for a decade. Maybe that’s an option, too.

But, hey, this is Tom Cruise. When he sets his mind on something, he achieves it. With that in mind, expect a dramatic upward turn in the quality of his interviews from this moment onwards. Thanks for reading. Please still send cakes.

Entertainment.title: A naked performance artist in the garden with her mum: Rona Bar and Ofek Avshalom’s best photograph
Entertainment.text:
This photograph is of Lois and Carey, who we found while looking for subjects for our project Proof of Existence. That series involved transforming models into surreal or exaggerated characters based on aspects of themselves, then photographing them in everyday settings. We got in contact with Lois after seeing her work on Instagram. When we went to her house and met her mother, Carey, we became very intrigued by the two of them, by their relationship and by the house itself.

The intention of that initial photo was to show how they express their Jewish identity in a non-traditional way. Lois and Carey are artists and their house is full of art. It was amazing to see how the things they’re interested in seem almost to spill out of their bodies and on to the walls, in the form of artwork, motifs and symbols. Their story is everywhere; it feels like the house itself is alive.

The way they express their Judaism was something we hadn’t encountered before. Lois is involved in performance art, and the fetish community, and her art deals with sexuality and queerness. In that first photo, she’s standing in the kitchen wearing a latex mask and bodysuit featuring the Star of David, while Carey sits drawing at the table behind her. It’s a striking example of one of the themes of the series – how heritage is passed on from one generation to another, being reinvented every time.

That photograph became the starting point for a new project, focusing entirely on Lois and Carey and their home. They welcomed us with open arms and it was very easy to work with them, so we just kept going. They gave us completely free rein, and two years after meeting them, we would still be finding new rooms, new walls, new knick-knacks. One of our favourite photographs is of Lois’s abandoned childhood bedroom, with its bright pink fireplace contrasting with the peeling walls.

The garden is as impressive as the house’s interior. Carey is obsessed with it and takes care of it daily. Another thing we like to explore in our work is contrast – ordinary acts with an aspect of absurdity or weirdness that provokes or intrigues the viewer and makes them wonder. The pose they are in here is obviously staged, but represents an emotional truth – the unique connection and coexistence of the two. The garden is an extension and symbol of the relationship, in a way. Carey is watering her plants, and Lois is just there in between them, almost as if she is one of them.

In some of the photographs, we also see Carey naked. The pair of them are very comfortable being nude around one another, completely relaxed and unguarded, but their closeness is mostly unspoken. They won’t say “I love you” or be very touchy, but they do demonstrate their closeness in other ways. For example, one of our photographs shows Lois tattooing her mother, which is a very intimate act. She does that all the time: it’s as if Carey acts as a canvas for her daughter’s art.

Certain themes, such as relationships, individualities and the home as an extension of identity, run through much of our work, which we do under the name Fotómetro. Our first joint long-term project, Us, was started in Tel Aviv and completed in London after we moved there in 2022. After collaborating a few years before, we’d realised we liked the work we did together more than our individual projects, and later we became a couple. Partly inspired by our own relationship, Us involved taking portraits of couples in their homes. People’s homes say so much about them.

Our association with Lois and Carey quickly became a friendship – sometimes, we would visit them without even taking the camera. Even since the series became a book, they continue to inspire us. We’re currently working on two films – one about Lois and one about Carey.

Born: Israel, 1995

High points: Exhibiting at the National Portrait Gallery in London as part of the 2023 Taylor Wessing Photography prize (we will exhibit there again in November – Lois and Carey in the Garden has been chosen for this year’s Winston Taylor Photo Portrait prize). Presenting our solo exhibition, Proof of Existence, at Cicek Gallery, London, in 2025. Winning the Eve Arnold Photography prize in 2025 with our series Lois and Carey. Publishing two photobooks: Us with Snap Collective in 2022, and Lois & Carey with 89Books in 2026. Exhibiting at Photo London 2026 with Bright Gallery

Top tips: The most important work is the never-ending process of personal exploration and developing your own artistic voice. The photographs you choose to make and the stories you choose to tell should feel like a calling – something you genuinely need to explore and communicate. An artist should constantly ask themselves: what do I want to say? How do I want to say it? And, most importantly, why do I need to say it? This process of questioning, experimenting and discovering your own perspective is far more important than technique, equipment or following trends. Those things can be learned and acquired, but developing a voice that is truly your own takes time, curiosity and continuous exploration.

Fotómetro’s Lois and Carey series will be exhibited at the Head On Photo festival in Sydney, Australia, in November. To see work by Lois Ward-Marvin and Carey Marvin, visit @lois.spookedd and @c.s.marvin

Entertainment.title: The secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed?
Entertainment.text:
It’s a question that has taxed musical thinkers for centuries: just what is it about one composer’s music that makes it more distinctive than anyone else’s? Entire disciplines of academic thought, of music analysis and historical musicology, as well as the formation of classical music’s canon of “great” composers, have been given over to this single idea: can it be proved that Mozart, say, was measurably “better” than other composers?

Our instinctive feeling about the sensual magic of Mozart’s music is part of the equation, but accounting for precisely how his pieces can sustain a lifetime of listening, why their pleasures never seem to pall and are still capable of seeming to surprise us even when we know them inside out: that’s the million-dollar musicological question.

What generations of music analysts have tried and largely failed to do through imperfect means of variously subjective techniques, an 18-year-old US student has managed to prove through a combination of data and interpretative ingenuity.

A recent study by Philadelphia student Linus Chen-Plotkin demonstrates that Mozart’s melodies are more surprising in the way they unfold, moment-by-moment and note-by-note, than those of his contemporaries and successors, Haydn, Beethoven and Schubert.

Chen-Plotkin put 600 movements of these four composers’ piano sonatas and string quartets through his bespoke software to analyse their tunes, based on Markov chains and other statistical and mathematical tools (he explains his work here). The data revealed that Mozart’s tunes have a shorter “memory” than other composers. That means the way they move is less predictable: that Mozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies and ideas that he confounds rather than confirms.

You can instinctively hear that at work in so many moments of his string quartets: the opening idea of the E flat major quartet, K428, which is already slipping out of the realms of the expected as early as its third note; or the opening of the Dissonance Quartet, K465, whose entire introduction is a chain of ever-more surprising moves of melody and harmony.

Chen-Plotkin is circumspect about the consequences of his work, recognising its limits as well as its possibilities. In fact, his statistical analyses shore up the conclusions that musicologists have often made about Mozart’s music: that it’s dizzyingly rich and strange in how it moves from note to note and phrase to phrase, but that Mozart was less interested in finding new or unpredictable structures across entire movements. In fact, if Chen-Plotkin were looking at unpredictability across whole pieces and not at the smaller scale of individual tunes and melodies, he would probably have come up with very different results: my hunch at least would be that Beethoven and Haydn would win those contests.

Mind you, Chen-Plotkin isn’t suggesting that maths replaces musicology. As well as being against the use of generative AI in art-making, his ambition is simply to show how statistical analysis can help reveal the underlying patterns behind human creativity. And his work has just begun: he enrols at university this autumn, and has already embarked on a computational analysis of the works and words of Chaucer.

Anyway: I’m back to put more Mozart through the random note generator of my fingers as I try – and fail, yet again – to play even one movement of his piano sonatas without making a mistake that not even Chen-Plotkin’s software or Markov’s chains could predict.

The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra is 80 this week, and, as you can see on their anniversary timeline, there’s a lot to celebrate. Which other orchestra can claim a legacy that encompasses some of the most exciting performances of Sibelius ever recorded in the 1950s and 60s? Listen to their founder Thomas Beecham’s performance of Tapiola to hear the edge of orchestral possibility, just as Sibelius pushes his music to new limits of wildness and experimentalism. Then, in the orchestra’s years with Rudolf Kempe in the 60s and early 70s, it transformed London’s musical life, and made pioneering recordings such as Janáček’s Glagolitic Mass.

But this is also the orchestra that Beecham insisted was men-only for as long as he conducted them (until his death in 1961), and which only had its first female musician over a decade later – clarinettist Prudence Whittaker.

It’s also the same ensemble who would find new dimensions of orchestral kitsch with Hooked on Classics in the 1980s, who recorded the Champions League theme in the 90s, and played at King Charles’s coronation in the 2020s; and it’s the orchestra that played this summer with Mandle Cheung, who paid an undisclosed amount to conduct Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony.

The RPO have soundtracked the decades from the sublime to the ridiculous; and they’ve surfed financial crisis after crisis over the years. Under Vasily Petrenko’s music directorship since 2021, here’s hoping the sublime continues to win out.

Entertainment.title: ‘We weren’t shy. We were queers in leather!’ Sunil Gupta on his momentous photographs of gay life
Entertainment.text:
‘I’ve been very promiscuous,” Sunil Gupta says, reflecting on his experiments with photography since the 1970s. Gupta, who was born in India, brought up in Canada and moved to the UK in 1978 after two years studying in New York, has documented and described queer lives for five decades. In his work, he’s quietly tried to find new ways of seeing, exploring the potential of photography to blur fiction and reality, public space and intimate, clandestine moments. His work explores the ways we love and relate to one another, set against the ever-shifting tides of politics and society.

He photographs with love – but it hasn’t been without risk. An exhibition in India was once shut down by the government, and in his early days in the UK, when he was working with fellow photographer Tessa Boffin, he recalls curators “physically shrinking away when we walked in the room – two queers in leather were too much for them! But we were quite aggressively upfront with our sexualities, we weren’t shy about it.”

Ahead of his retrospective exhibition at Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge, Gupta talks through 10 landmark images from across his career.

1. No 43 from Christopher Street

This is almost the only photograph in this series that prominently features a person of colour; it was unusual to see Asian people on Christopher Street in New York at the time, and I saw myself a little bit in the person on the right. These two in the foreground are very much what I remember from that time: you get the hair and clothes because you want to look the part, and you find someone to hang out with. Behind them is the counterfoil: the regular gay guys who parade up and down Christopher Street – but here, they’re in the background. I also like the lone figure further down the street – there’s something about the loneliness of cruising on the street.

2. From Towards an Indian Gay Image

This picture is defining because I’d gone back to Delhi for the first time. I had grown up next to this tomb, which is why it keeps reappearing in the work. I was trying to find a way of photographing gay men in Delhi, but this was circa 1982 – nobody would be in a picture. There was complete silence around the subject of homosexuality. Even people who went out to have sex in public places – there was no chitchat, no language around it. So I began to take headless pictures but it wasn’t really going anywhere. But I liked this, and it made my degree show at the RCA. When I graduated, my livelihood was freelancing. I went to The Guardian, and they said, is there a story? I said yes, then I ran home and wrote a story and they published it in the paper – so it is also my first published picture.

3. From Trespass Series 1

I made these montages on the first Apple computers that had lo-res scanners, I had a lot of fun with it. I printed them very big in a coffee shop in Soho. The discussion at that time, in 1992, was the opposite of Brexit – should we go into the single European currency? The left then was quite anti the euro, and it raised a lot of questions for migrants from the Commonwealth – we thought we would lose our right to be here. In this series I imagined Germany as the centre of a united Europe – geographically and economically.

4. From ‘Pretended’ Family Relationships

This began as a project about Clause 28, [later Section 28, a law introduced by Thatcher’s government in 1988 that banned local authorities and schools from “promoting homosexuality”]. In the late 1980s, I was living in a bubble in Brixton, with a white partner, and all the couples we knew were multiracial, and we thought that was cool and how it should be. I began to shoot but it was hard to get Black and Asian models to be in queer stuff in pictures, no one could be out. So they were fake couples, people I knew.

5. From Love and Light

This marked my return to India in 2005. I had met this person in Leh, who was in film and theatre. He was a guru as well. We got together, it was very intense. I turned up in India with my suitcase, by which time he had lost interest. But I thought I would stay. The plan had been to make a series of pictures of us together in various interesting locations – instead it turned into just me in various interesting locations. And then at the end, I met my husband, Charan Singh, at an Aids conference in Delhi. He was a social worker and I was on stage as a person with HIV.

6. From Country: Portrait of an Indian Village (taken in 2007)

In London, you walk out and no one knows you. Then you go to this village in India and everyone knows who you are, who your grandfather was, how you arrived. After a few weeks it’s quite claustrophobic. I thought I’d make a project about a village in Rajasthan and I got very involved with it but it was as an outsider. But in this place, I wander around with a camera, I stop and chat. An uncle gave me a 300-year oral history. My cousin has built me a horrible concrete bunker on my father’s small piece of land which he thinks I might like to live in, which is very sweet of him. I guess if everything went belly up I could be there in the bunker.

7. From Sun City (main image)

This is based on a scene from Chris Marker’s La Jettée. It’s a coming together of a gay photo history I was never taught but I gathered for myself. Each person’s pose references a different historic image – from Robert Mapplethorpe to George Platt Lynes back to Wilhelm Von Gloeden and French Romantic painting.

8. From the Black Experience

This was part of a show at [London gallery] Autograph in 1986, commissioned by the Greater London Council. The idea of Black then was anybody with heritage that came from a form of British empire – the GLC’s early definitions even included the Irish. I found myself with two struggles – Asians who didn’t think they were Black, and Black colleagues who weren’t looking at Asian culture at all. I thought if I didn’t make the pictures about South Asians there would be no images of us in the show – I made 10 pictures. That exhibition was the start of Autograph. It’s incredible it’s still there.

I was at a very low point. I was approaching 50. I’d been diagnosed with HIV, my work had gone down and my social life had gone. I got a three-year fellowship in Southampton, which was quite extraordinary. I made this project about me as a person with HIV looking at the landscape and where I had come from. These pictures were both made in London; one is in St Thomas’ hospital where I have my treatments, and the unpleasant experience of having a reverse drip coming out of my heart. The other image is on Drummond Street, where I would go to an Indian food place.

In 1986-7 I got a commission from the Photographers’ Gallery in London. I thought I’d use it to go back to Delhi and do a project about Indian gay men. My informants took me to the places they went cruising and agreed to be in the pictures, up to a point. I would chat to many more people just with a tape recorder. The extracts are from the recordings but they don’t always match the person in the picture. I felt just pictures wouldn’t convey the complexity of what was going on.

I think part of my journey has been to put Indian gay men into cultural history. When I was a student you couldn’t find them anywhere. I’m so excited this work has now been acquired by MoMA in New York, so I feel they’re in the history books now. My job is done.

BreakingNewsTab.title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to be run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.

He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

A spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive".

"Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed," they said.

Brandram, who served as a Captain in the Scots Guards in Afghanistan, was working more recently in private banking for HSBC.

He is a distant relative of European royalty - his grandmother was Princess Katherine of Greece, and the late Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, was his father's godfather.

BreakingNewsTab.title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".

Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.

Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength".

She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".

Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.

Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.

"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.

Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.

In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.

But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.

Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.

Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.

In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.

Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.

Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato.

Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance.

But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4.

The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them.

Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.

Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.

Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.

A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.

The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach.

Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis.

Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected.

Human rights groups worry such a move would see vulnerable people, including women and children, turned back and denied the protection afforded to them under international law.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.

The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.

The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.

"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."

The White House and US Central Command have been approached for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.

One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.

The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.

At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.

A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.

The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what is likely to be the final such House vote ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teacher pay strike
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Schools in England are to get around £500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.

Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.

Daniel Kebede, the General Secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.

In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.

The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.

The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around £500m, which schools can now use towards teachers pay this year.

In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.

The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional £700m for 2026-27 and £1.1bn for the following year.

Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.

The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.

Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".

Paul Whiteman, General Secretary of the National Association of Headteachers, said the decision is "certainly welcome", putting schools in a "better position".

He said his union would look carefully at the detail "to determine whether this means the pay uplift is genuinely fully funded" for schools.

In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.

A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.

The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.

A spokesperson for Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government was "confident schools can now meet the costs of the award at a national level".

"The Secretary of State has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on Diana stolen in the Netherlands
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

The BBC understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

Dutch police said they were aware of the incident and have been approached for comment.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be released in the UK and globally on Tuesday, and tells the story of Princess Diana's life from the Earl's perspective.

A source said the truck driver was taking a mandatory break in a car park and was sleeping in his cab at the time the books were stolen.

They added Dutch police are investigating. They did not say where the theft took place.

The Daily Mail, who first reported the theft, external and is serialising the book, said the theft took place earlier this week in the Dutch countryside.

The book's publisher Penguin Michael Joseph - a division of Penguin Random House - and Dutch publisher Overamstel, who have rights to the book in the Netherlands, were approached for comment by the BBC.

Princess Diana, who died aged 36 following a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.

Her sons Prince William and Prince Harry were aged 15 and 12 respectively at the time of her death.

Last month announcing the book's publication, Earl Spencer explained ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death he had been inundated with interview requests and he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than "having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others".

"The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother's perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral," he added, referring to the eulogy he delivered in Westminster Abbey in September 1997.

"I want to speak on Diana's behalf and do so in an openly positive way."

In his eulogy, Earl Spencer described Princess Diana as the "very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty", adding: "All over the world she was a symbol of selfless humanity... a standard bearer for the rights of the truly downtrodden."

He also used the speech to criticise the media, calling her the "most hunted person of the modern age" and pledged to protect Prince William and Prince Harry and prevent them suffering a similar fate.

In 2023, copies of Prince Harry's memoir Spare were accidentally put on sale in Spain days ahead of the official global release.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Former Cambridgeshire officer jailed for 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
BreakingNewsTab.text:
An ex-police sergeant who asked to share a female suspect's sex video with "the lads from footy" has been jailed for four years.

Former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street, 41, engaged in "salacious gossip" with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman's personal phone.

The Old Bailey heard how Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, created a "toxic" WhatsApp culture at work. He was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office.

Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: "The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime."

On Wednesday, the woman told of her "overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation" as Street was sentenced.

The court also heard Street encouraged colleagues in WhatsApp messages to "bully" a teenage detainee.

Street admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to confidential information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020.

During sentencing, the judge described his actions as "both appalling and inexplicable", adding: "I am sure there will be many thousands of officers in police forces in this country and abroad utterly horrified by your actions and by the attitude you have each displayed here."

Lucraft noted the "collateral impact" of Street's offending, with 67 cases he was connected with being discontinued - and a further 14 now under review.

Williams, 38, also of Huntingdon, who admitted misconduct in public office, was handed a 16-month prison sentence.

Street had appeared in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting "impressive results" through his "robust" style.

However, in November 2021, an anti-corruption team seized his mobile phones for examination as part of an audit of Cambridgeshire officers and staff.

The offences were committed while he was leading a unit at Cambourne police station, dealing mainly with county lines and organised crime.

During the trial, prosecutor Anne Whyte KC described how Street created a "toxic culture" which led to investigations into 11 other officers.

In April 2020, Street called on his team to "bully" a 17-year-old detainee, encouraging them to "please hit him" and "smash his head in".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Neuroscientists in the US have successfully adapted mice to have functioning human cells inside their own brains.

The researchers hope that potential treatments for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diseases that only occur in humans could now be tested on the laboratory rodents.

While mice with brains that are partly human might sound like a Kafkaesque experiment, the scientists said these are not "mice that think like humans".

The animals are genetically engineered - and surgically altered - so that some of their brain tissue is human.

The scientists said their work, published in the journal Nature, external, was carried out with independent ethical scrutiny.

The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.

Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do.

As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials".

"Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."

The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".

Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."

The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.

While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents, external, these scientists took that approach to a new level.

First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.

The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue.

These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.

When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.

The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".

After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.

About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.

Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did".

"They don't have any enhancement," he added.

Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."

But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition".

"How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.

Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".

In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice.

"You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.

These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders.

Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".

This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".

Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer.

"So this is a new avenue."
